idiom_name: functools.singledispatch with a registered implementation per element type
implementation_notes: An operation over a type set is just a function in Python, and functools.singledispatch turns a plain function into a generic one whose implementations are registered per argument type, so adding an operation is a new function and the elements stay untouched. The classic second dispatch disappears because the operation is chosen before the call: only the element's type is still unknown. Registering on an abstract base class gives the visitor's subtyping behaviour (the nearest registered ancestor wins), and the base implementation should raise so an unregistered type fails loudly - singledispatch registers the base function under object, which otherwise answers for every type. Use singledispatchmethod (3.8+) for methods, since a plain decorator cannot dispatch on self. The standard library's own visitor, ast.NodeVisitor, is the same idea with the operation as a class, dispatching reflectively on the node class name and never asking the elements for accept().
pitfalls: The base implementation is registered for object, so an unregistered type silently gets the fallback; raise NotImplementedError there unless a catch-all answer is genuinely correct.

Dispatch happens on the first argument only, and it is cached: registering implementations later (or registering ABCs that change subclass relationships) invalidates the cache but can change earlier decisions.
singledispatchmethod is required for instance methods - decorating a method with plain singledispatch dispatches on self and never finds the right implementation.
Registration happens at import time, so a module that is never imported registers nothing; keep operations importable (or register explicitly) instead of relying on side effects.

variants.name: Structural pattern matching (match/case) over a closed union
variants.idiom_name: match statement with class patterns over dataclasses
variants.implementation_notes: Python 3.10's match statement dispatches on structure and type in one construct, so a closed set of dataclasses is handled by one function per operation with a case arm per shape; it reads like the functional-language answer to the expression problem (types closed, operations open) and needs no registration machinery. The language does not check exhaustiveness, so the case _ arm must raise (or call typing.assert_never) for an unhandled type to fail immediately. Choose match when one operation benefits from seeing the whole shape of a node at once and when the node set is defined next to the operation; choose singledispatch when operations live in separate modules and are registered from outside.
variants.code_sketch:
# elements: @dataclass Num(value) and @dataclass Add(left, right)

def evaluate(node):
    match node:
        case Num(value=v):         return v
        case Add(left=l, right=r): return evaluate(l) + evaluate(r)
        case _: raise TypeError(f"no evaluate rule for {type(node).__name__}")
pitfalls: match is not exhaustive: without a case _ that raises, an added node type returns None and the bug surfaces far from the operation.
Class patterns test with isinstance and take the first matching arm, so a base-class arm above a subclass arm shadows it with no diagnostic.
Patterns bind by attribute lookup (dataclasses also support positional patterns through __match_args__), so reordering dataclass fields silently changes positional matches.
match on very hot paths has overhead compared with a dict dispatch; benchmark before replacing a table lookup.

variants.name: ast.NodeVisitor / ast.NodeTransformer reflective dispatch
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's visitor for the Python AST: subclass ast.NodeVisitor, define visit_<ClassName> methods and call visit(tree). Dispatch is reflective - the node class name selects the method, generic_visit is the fallback - and the traversal lives in the framework, so an operation overrides only the node kinds it cares about and ast.NodeTransformer adds node replacement on the way back up. This is the classic visitor minus accept() (the element classes are never modified) and minus one operation class per type, which is how it scales to a hundred-plus node classes. Use it, or copy its shape, when the hierarchy is generated or must stay untouched and the operation is a class with per-instance state; it also works as the documented way to write AST lint rules.
variants.code_sketch:
import ast

class NameCollector(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.names = []
    def visit_Name(self, node):          # reflective: class name -> method
        self.names.append(node.id)
        self.generic_visit(node)         # keep descending

collector = NameCollector()
collector.visit(ast.parse("x = y + 1"))
pitfalls: Forgetting generic_visit() prunes the subtree silently - fewer results, no error.
Dispatch is by class name, so a renamed or version-specific node type falls back to generic_visit instead of failing; pin the Python version you support.
The visitor has no compile-time or runtime completeness check: overriding nothing is a valid visitor that visits everything and does nothing.
State lives on the visitor instance, so one collector cannot be reused for two trees without being reset - or use a fresh instance per traversal.
